comments.author: @HugeManBeingOfficial
comments.text:
Great video, Geoff! As a born-and-raised Oregonian, here are a few deep-cut local nuggets to go with the "54°40' or Fight!" segment:

 It's really "ore-GONE": Locals love correcting out-of-staters, but the name traces back to the Ouragon River—from the French ouragan ("hurricane") for those brutal Columbia Gorge winds.

 A dead trapper built our government: In 1841, settlers only formed a provisional government because wealthy trapper Ewing Young died without a will and they needed a probate court to divvy up his estate.

 French Prairie was here first: Before the wagon trains, a tiny group of French-Canadian trappers held down the valley, spoke French to the U.S. envoy, and nearly voted down an American government at Champoeg in 1843.

16:11 -- Mount Shasta isn't the end of Cascadia. Mount Lassen is the southernmost volcanic peak in the range.

replies.author: @Mike-kc5ew
replies.text: As far as the drainage basin, it all flows into the Pacific, except for the far southeastern part of the state. It's also specifically a part of the old Oregon territory and was included in the treaty of 1846. Regionally I see people make the argument that it's a part of the inter-mountain West, but that's a very large disconnected area, where Idaho has an entirely different watershed region from any of the other states defined as inter-mountain. There are some who incorrectly call it Great Basin, which other than the southeastern part, it's not. That's mostly Utah and Nevada. Culturally Idaho is more in line with Utah, Wyoming, and Montana, but cultures are known well to change over time, so defining it by culture is about as steady as checking which way the wind is blowing. Many right leaning Idahoans don't like being lumped in with the left coast, but you get down to what Idaho is, and it really is mostly defined as inland Northwest, which would be a sub-region of the PNW.
